summary.overview: Chapter 1 establishes the book's vocabulary for reasoning about data-intensive systems. It explains why modern applications are composed from databases, caches, search indexes, stream-processing systems, and batch-processing systems; why combining those components effectively makes the application itself a data system; and how to evaluate that system through reliability, scalability, and maintainability. Reliability is analyzed through hardware faults, systematic software faults, and human error. Scalability is framed as a workload-specific question using load parameters, the Twitter timeline fan-out example, response-time distributions, percentiles, tail latency, and scaling strategies. Maintainability is divided into operability, simplicity, and evolvability.

data_intensive.definition: The primary challenge is data quantity, data complexity, or the speed at which data changes, rather than raw CPU.

building_blocks.cache: Remember expensive results to speed reads.

blurred_categories: Redis can act as both datastore and message queue.
Apache Kafka has message-queue/log behavior with database-like durability.
data_intensive.composite_system: When application code combines several general-purpose data tools behind one API, it effectively creates a special-purpose data system and becomes responsible for cross-component guarantees such as cache invalidation.

reliability.definition: Continue working correctly, at required performance, even when things go wrong.
working_correctly_includes: Meet required performance under expected load.
reliability.fault: One component deviates from its specification.
reliability.failure: The system as a whole stops providing the required service.
reliability.fault_tolerance_goal: Prevent component faults from becoming system failures.
reliability.chaos_testing: Deliberately trigger faults to continuously exercise recovery; Netflix Chaos Monkey is the example.

hardware_faults.cluster_implication: At 10,000 disks, expect roughly one disk failure per day.
hardware_faults.modern_direction: Use software fault tolerance to survive loss of whole machines, enabling rolling upgrades.

software_faults.characteristic: Often systematic and correlated across nodes.
examples: One bad input crashes all application-server instances.
Dependency slows, hangs, or returns corrupted responses.
mitigations: Think carefully about assumptions and interactions.

human_errors.observation: The cited study found operator configuration errors were the leading outage cause; hardware contributed to only 10–25% of outages.

scalability.definition: Having reasonable strategies for coping with a specific increase in load.

twitter_example.fanout_on_read: Store each tweet once; assemble timeline at read time. Cheap writes, expensive reads.
twitter_example.fanout_on_write: Copy each tweet into followers' home-timeline caches. Expensive writes, cheap reads.
twitter_example.celebrity_extreme: Some users have more than 30 million followers.
twitter_example.hybrid: Fan out ordinary users on write; fetch celebrity tweets at read time and merge them.
twitter_example.key_load_parameter: Follower-count distribution, potentially weighted by tweet frequency.

performance.throughput: Common batch metric: records processed per second or total job time.
performance.response_time: Client-visible time from request submission to receiving the response.
performance.latency: Time a request spends waiting to be handled.
amazon_examples: p99.9 used for some internal response-time requirements.
The chapter cites 100 ms additional response time reducing sales by 1%.
p99.99 optimization was considered too expensive for the benefit.

queueing_and_tail_amplification.head_of_line_blocking: A few slow requests occupy limited processing capacity and delay requests queued behind them.
queueing_and_tail_amplification.load_test_rule: A load generator should issue requests independently of prior response completion.
queueing_and_tail_amplification.tail_latency_amplification: An end-user request that fans out to many backends waits for the slowest call, increasing the chance of a slow overall response.
queueing_and_tail_amplification.aggregation_rule: Do not average percentiles; aggregate histograms.

scaling_approaches.vertical: Scale up to a more powerful machine.
scaling_approaches.horizontal: Scale out across multiple machines; also called shared-nothing.
scaling_approaches.elastic: Automatically add resources as load changes.
scaling_approaches.manual: Humans analyze capacity and add resources.
important_tradeoffs: Real systems often use a pragmatic mixture of vertical and horizontal scaling.
Elasticity helps unpredictable load; manual scaling can be simpler and less surprising.
Stateful distributed systems add much more complexity than stateless services.
There is no one-size-fits-all scalable architecture.
scaling_approaches.premature_scaling_warning: Early-stage products may benefit more from fast iteration than from scaling to hypothetical future load.

maintainability.why_it_matters: Most software cost occurs after initial development during operation, debugging, adaptation, technical-debt repayment, and new features.
maintainability.operability: Make routine operation and failure recovery easy.
maintainability.simplicity: Make systems easy to understand by reducing complexity.
maintainability.evolvability: Make systems easy to modify as requirements change.

system_support: Self-healing plus manual control when needed.

simplicity.accidental_complexity: Implementation complexity that is not inherent in the user-visible problem.
examples: SQL hides storage structures, concurrency, and crash-recovery details.

evolvability.definition: Ease of adapting a data system to changing requirements; also called extensibility, modifiability, or plasticity.
evolvability.relationship_to_simplicity: Simple systems with good abstractions are usually easier to change.

scenario_questions.scenario: A service uses a DB, Redis cache, Elasticsearch, and Kafka behind one API.
scenario_questions.question: What chapter concept is illustrated?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A composite/special-purpose data system assembled from general-purpose components.

scenario_questions.scenario: A database write succeeds but the cache remains stale.
scenario_questions.question: What guarantee must the composite system provide?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Correct cache invalidation/update so clients see consistent results.

scenario_questions.scenario: One node crashes but users see no interruption.
scenario_questions.question: Fault or failure?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A component fault occurred, but the system avoided a failure.

scenario_questions.scenario: A team randomly kills service processes to verify failover.
scenario_questions.question: What practice is this?

scenario_questions.scenario: One malformed request crashes every server instance.
scenario_questions.question: Why is this dangerous?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: It is a systematic/correlated software fault capable of causing widespread failure.

scenario_questions.question: Why can fan-out-on-write become problematic?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: One post can create over 30M timeline writes.

scenario_questions.question: What tradeoff favors fan-out-on-write?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Doing more work during less-frequent writes makes frequent reads much cheaper.

scenario_questions.scenario: A service reports only mean latency.
scenario_questions.question: What should be added?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Response-time percentiles such as p50/p95/p99/p999 and tail latency.

scenario_questions.question: Interpret it.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: 95% of requests are faster than 1.5s; 5% take 1.5s or longer.

scenario_questions.scenario: One frontend request calls 20 backends in parallel.
scenario_questions.question: Why can it be slow?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Tail-latency amplification: it waits for the slowest backend call.

scenario_questions.scenario: A benchmark waits for every response before sending the next request.
scenario_questions.question: Why is this unrealistic?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: It artificially suppresses queueing and understates real-world tail latency.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two workloads move the same bytes/sec but have radically different request sizes/frequencies.
scenario_questions.question: Should architecture be the same?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: No. Workload shape, access patterns, and latency requirements may require different architectures.

scenario_questions.question: What maintainability principle is weak?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Operability; improve monitoring, documentation, automation, and predictable controls.

scenario_questions.scenario: A codebase has tangled dependencies and many special-case hacks.
scenario_questions.question: What concept applies?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Accidental complexity; simplicity and abstraction should be improved.

short_answer_questions.question: Why group databases, caches, queues, and indexes as data systems?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Their traditional categories increasingly overlap, and modern applications often combine several tools to satisfy one system's storage and processing requirements.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain fault vs failure.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A fault is a component deviation; a failure is system-level loss of required service. Fault tolerance attempts to contain faults before users experience failure.

short_answer_questions.question: Why can software faults be harder than hardware faults?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They are often systematic and correlated, so the same trigger can affect many nodes simultaneously or cascade across dependencies.

short_answer_questions.question: How should systems account for human error?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Use safe interfaces, sandboxes, testing, gradual deployment, rollback, telemetry, recomputation tools, and training.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain Twitter's hybrid feed strategy.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Most tweets are fanned out into follower caches at write time, while celebrity tweets are fetched and merged at read time to avoid extreme write amplification.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are percentiles better than averages for response time?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Response time is a distribution; percentiles reveal typical and tail experiences that a mean can hide.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain tail-latency amplification.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A user request that fans out to many backends completes only after the slowest call, so the chance of encountering a slow outlier grows with fan-out.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare vertical, horizontal, elastic, and manual scaling.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Vertical uses stronger machines; horizontal uses more machines; elastic scaling adjusts automatically; manual scaling relies on human capacity decisions.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is there no one-size-fits-all scalable architecture?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Reads, writes, request size/frequency, data volume/complexity, access patterns, and latency requirements differ across applications.

short_answer_questions.question: What makes software maintainable?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Operability makes it easy to run, simplicity reduces complexity, and evolvability makes future change easier.
